evidence: In the GDPval setup, GPT-5 high had web search, code interpreter, and a file-capable container available, but many failures were observable formatting defects in generated deliverables: black-square PDF artifacts and egregious PowerPoint formatting errors. The intervention in §3.4/App. A.3 explicitly instructed the agent to render visual deliverables to PNGs, inspect them, run programmatic formatting checks, and verify submitted files; after this, multimodal inspection rose from 15% to 97%, black-square artifacts were eliminated, and PowerPoint formatting errors decreased though did not disappear.
reasoning: The root issue was not malformed tool arguments or a nonexistent tool call, and there was no explicit tool error whose feedback the model ignored. The closest fit is Incorrect Tool Selection because the model failed to select/use the available tool path needed for the task—rendering and inspecting generated files via the container/multimodal workflow—before submitting visual deliverables.

I read the GDPval paper source material, especially §3.4 “Increasing Reasoning Effort and Scaffolding” and Appendix A.3. The reference is not a single step-by-step trajectory log; it is an aggregate experimental report about GPT-5/GPT-5 high behavior on GDPval tasks and a prompt/scaffolding intervention. Below is a chronological account limited to facts stated or directly implied by that source.

## Chronological account

GDPval evaluated models on real-world economically valuable tasks created by industry professionals. Each task consisted of a request, often with reference files, and a requested deliverable/work product. The benchmark included multimodal and file-based work such as spreadsheets, documents, presentations, images, video, audio, diagrams, slide decks, and specialized file formats.

For the OpenAI model runs, the authors report that they enabled the web search tool and the code interpreter tool, with background sampling. They also preinstalled many packages in the production Docker image and made these packages available to the agent during OpenAI sampling. Appendix A.6.4 lists packages such as LibreOffice, python-pptx, PyMuPDF, pandas, matplotlib, pytesseract, moviepy, pydub, ffmpeg-python, scikit-image, reportlab, openpyxl, xlrd, and others. The paper states that these tools and packages were intended to help the model process GDPval’s broad range of file types.

The model under discussion was evaluated as part of GDPval’s OpenAI model experiments. The paper refers to “GPT-5 high” rather than “GPT-5-xhigh,” but the referenced setup matches the described OpenAI sampling harness: web search and code interpreter enabled, background sampling, and a file-capable container environment.

Before the prompt/scaffolding intervention described in §3.4, the authors analyzed model strengths and weaknesses. In §3.3, they report that GPT-5 high lost mainly because of formatting errors, while having relatively fewer instruction-following issues than Claude, Gemini, and Grok. They also state that GPT-5 and Grok showed the fewest accuracy errors, though all models sometimes hallucinated data or miscalculated. In this earlier evaluation context, expert graders preferred human deliverables over model deliverables in many cases because models failed to fully follow instructions on GDPval tasks.

The authors then investigated whether increased reasoning effort and additional scaffolding would improve performance. They ran GDPval on o3 and GPT-5 at low, medium, and high reasoning effort and found that additional reasoning effort improved performance. Separately, they created a prompt to elicit better GPT-5 behavior on GDPval-style multimodal economic tasks.

The prompt in Appendix A.3 gave the agent detailed production and formatting instructions. It told the agent not to use the en dash character U+2011, and instead to use the normal hyphen U+002D. It also told the agent to avoid emojis, nonstandard bullet points, and other special characters unless there was an extremely good reason, because such characters might render poorly on some computers.

The prompt instructed the agent to ensure graphics embedded in PDFs or slides were large enough to be legible, generally at least half a page wide, but not so large that they became ugly or cut off. It recommended plots, charts, and simple graphics, while warning that complicated visuals made by overlaying shapes on images often appeared unprofessional.

For PDFs, the prompt specifically instructed the agent to always use LibreOffice to create the PDF, saying it “must be LibreOffice,” and that if LibreOffice was not installed, the agent could install it. The prompt said other libraries sometimes produced weird artifacts on some computers. For fonts, it instructed the agent to use cross-platform fonts, recommending Noto Sans or Noto Serif unless there was a strong reason to use another font, and to embed any nonstandard font in the source document.

The prompt also gave instructions about the final deliverable text. It told the agent not to link to submitted files in the deliverable text, because such links were not supported in the viewing interface. It said the ideal deliverable text should be concise, at most four sentences, and without unnecessary fluff. It emphasized that any files requested by the user should be actual files in the container, not only text in the response. If part of a task was unsolvable, for example because internet access was unavailable, the agent should mention that in the deliverable text. The submission should be complete and self-contained, and even if the model could not fully complete the task due to environmental limitations, it should still produce as complete a solution as possible.

The prompt told the agent to avoid excess verbosity: be clear and comprehensive, but avoid extra verbosity where possible. It also gave default filetype guidance: if the task did not request a specific filetype, the agent should use “standard” filetypes such as PDF, PPTX, DOCX, XLSX, MP4, ZIP, etc. For video files, it instructed the agent to extract a string of images and check those images to see whether visual elements were corrupted.

The prompt then required mandatory formatting checks before submission. First, the agent had to convert all visual deliverables to PNGs using LibreOffice, including PPTX, DOCX, PDF, and XLSX files. Each page or slide had to become a separate PNG. This conversion was explicitly for checking only; the agent was still supposed to submit the original deliverables in the requested original formats, unless the task had asked for PNGs.

Second, the agent had to display the PNGs and look for visible problems: text or graphics being cut off, overlapping, distorted, blank, unreadable, too dark on a light background, or too light on a dark background. It was told to look at each image thoroughly, zooming in if necessary, and to remember that the displayed image represented an entire slide or page, so any cutoff was an error in the deliverable.

Third, for highly visual submissions such as PPTX or PDF, the agent had to write programmatic formatting checks to ensure there were no blank pages, no text or graphics cut off the page, and no overlapping text or graphics except intentional overlaps. It also had to verify that page or slide limits were respected.

Fourth, the agent had to summarize the prompt’s deliverable instructions and match those instructions to the portion of the deliverable addressing them.

Fifth, immediately before submission, the agent had to check that the deliverables were exactly the files intended for submission, with no missing files and no extra files. It also had to check that each submitted file was not corrupted by opening it and verifying that it was well-formatted.

If any of the checks found a formatting issue, the prompt instructed the agent to fix the issue and repeat the checking process. The prompt emphasized that formatting errors were a “MAJOR ISSUE,” that the agent needed to fix them, that there was no time limit, and that it should go through the steps methodically. The final line of the response was required to be `CONFIDENCE[XX]`, with XX an integer from 0 to 100 indicating confidence that the submission was correct, followed instructions, and was well-formatted.

In addition to this prompt, §3.4 says the authors improved agent scaffolding by enabling GET requests in the container and by performing best-of-N sampling with N=4 and a GPT-5 judge. Appendix A.3 states that best-of-N sampling was performed by prompting a GPT-5 grader with the prompt, reference files, and deliverable files for four different submissions, then asking it to pick the best.

The source reports several feedback signals from these changes. Prompting fully eliminated black-square artifacts from GPT-5 responses; before the intervention, these artifacts had affected over half of generated PDFs. Prompting also reduced egregious formatting errors in PowerPoint files from 86% to 64%. The paper says this improvement can be partially attributed to a sharp increase in agents using multimodal capabilities to inspect deliverables, from 15% to 97%.

The final aggregate outcome was that prompting and scaffolding improved GPT-5 high performance. Figure 9b reports that GPT-5 high’s human-preference win rate increased from 38.8% to 43.1% with prompt tuning/scaffolding. The paper describes this as a 5 percentage point improvement. The authors conclude that these gains suggest paths to improving agents on GDPval tasks by training or scaffolding them to be more thorough and to use multimodal capabilities more fully.

At the same time, the reported outcome was not complete success. Even after the intervention, PowerPoint egregious formatting errors were reduced but not eliminated: they remained at 64%. GPT-5 high still did not reach the “parity with industry expert” line shown in the figures. The source therefore presents the failure pattern as one where GPT-5 high produced many otherwise plausible GDPval deliverables but often lost to human expert deliverables due to observable formatting problems, especially in visual/file-based outputs; the prompt and scaffolding improved but did not fully resolve those problems.
